theme: The LORD frustrates the plans of nations, sovereign over Babel
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 33:10-22 slowly, twice. This is the second half of Psalm 33, earlier in this plan we read verses 1-9, which praised God for creation. Today’s portion turns to God’s sovereignty over the nations and his particular care for his people. It is the perfect Psalm after the scattering of Babel.
settingTheScene:
Two days ago we read the tower of Babel, humanity united in pride against God, scattered in confusion. Today’s psalm gives us the divine perspective on the affairs of nations. From God’s vantage point, the schemes of humans are nothing. The plans of kings come to nothing apart from his will. And yet, the God who frustrates the proud also watches faithfully over those who fear him. This psalm is the right meditation after the events of Genesis 11.

We read Psalm 33:1-9 on an earlier day in this plan. That section celebrated creation by God’s word. Today’s half completes the meditation by showing that the same God who created by his word governs history by his sovereignty.
observation: Verse 10: “The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples.” Babel is exactly this, counsel of nations brought to nothing.
Verse 11: “The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations.” Contrast, human plans fail, God’s plans endure.
Verse 12: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage!” Election language, God chooses a people.
Verses 13-15: God looks down from heaven and sees ALL the children of man. He fashions their hearts. He observes their deeds.
Verses 16-17: “The king is not saved by his great army… the war horse is a false hope.” Military power is unreliable apart from God.
Verse 18: “Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love.” His attention is fixed on his people.
Verse 19: God delivers from death and keeps alive in famine. Common life-preservation under the Noahic Covenant.
Verses 20-22 close in waiting: “Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield.”
interpretation:
Psalm 33:10-22 picks up where the first half left off. Verses 1-9 praised God for creating by his word. Now the focus shifts to God’s sovereign rule over history, and to his particular care for the people who fear him.

Verse 10 lands with extra weight after our reading of Genesis 11. “The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples.” Babel is the paradigm example of this verse in action. Humanity united in counsel, “let us build a tower”, and God brought the counsel to nothing in a single act of language-confusion. The verse is not nostalgic about Babel; it is descriptive of God’s ongoing sovereignty. Every empire that has ever risen against God has eventually come to nothing. Babylon. Assyria. Persia. Rome. Every modern attempt to construct human autonomy apart from God ends in the same way, sooner or later, in confusion and scattering.

But the verse is followed immediately by its inverse. Verse 11: “The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations.” The same sovereignty that frustrates human plans establishes God’s plans. History is not a contest between God’s purposes and humanity’s purposes that might go either way. God’s plans are unshakeable. They will endure when every empire has fallen. This is not a depressing verse for the believer; it is the most hope-filled verse imaginable. The plans of God’s heart, including his plan to redeem you, to keep you, to bring you safely home, will stand forever.

Verse 12 then makes a particular claim: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage!” In Old Testament context, this referred primarily to Israel. But in the New Testament, the apostle Peter applies this language to the church: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). The church is now the people whom God has chosen as his heritage. The blessing of verse 12 belongs to every believer who is in Christ.

Verses 13-15 give us the vantage point of the King of heaven. “The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man; from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth.” Nothing escapes his gaze. Babel’s tower was not impressive to him; the present rebellions of contemporary humanity are not impressive to him either. From his throne, he sees everything, knows everything, fashions every heart, observes every deed. This is sobering for the wicked. It is comforting for the faithful. You are seen. By the God who matters.

Then verses 16-17 deliver one of the great political theology passages of the Psalter. “The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength. The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue.” This is a stunning claim in the ancient Near East. Every nation around Israel boasted in its military strength. Israel was tiny by comparison. And the psalmist says, plainly: military might does not save. Armies are not the deciding factor. War horses are not the source of victory. The Lord is. Whatever strength a king or nation has is temporary, contingent, and ultimately useless against the will of God.

Then verse 18 brings us to the warm center of the psalm. “Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love.” The same God whose eye sweeps over the whole earth has his eye fixed in particular on those who fear him. His attention is not divided thinly across humanity. It is concentrated on his people. Those who fear him, who hope in his steadfast love, they are watched, kept, loved with focused attention.

And what does God do for them? Verse 19: “that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.” This is the Noahic Covenant language at the personal level. God preserves life. He delivers from death. He keeps his people alive through times when others perish. This is true at the temporal level (sometimes God protects believers from physical disasters), and it is supremely true at the spiritual level (the eternal life he gives in Christ delivers from the second death and keeps the believer alive forever).

The psalm closes with a posture of waiting. “Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield. For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.” The Christian life is, in large part, a posture of waiting, waiting for promises to be fulfilled, for prayers to be answered, for the final consummation of all things. But it is not anxious waiting. It is glad waiting, trusting waiting, hoping waiting. We wait because we know whom we are waiting for.
connection: Today’s psalm is the divine perspective on yesterday’s reading. Where Genesis 11 showed us Babel from the ground, humans plotting, building, getting scattered, Psalm 33 shows us Babel from heaven. God sees the counsel of the nations and brings it to nothing. His own counsel stands forever. And while he scatters the proud, his eye remains on those who fear him. The psalm anticipates everything Unit 3 will develop. God is about to bring the counsel of his heart to bear in human history by calling one man, Abram. From Abram will come Israel, the “nation whose God is the LORD” (verse 12), the heritage God has chosen. And from Israel will come Christ, in whom the chosen heritage now includes every nation that believes.
application:
Live today in the light of God’s sovereignty. Two specific applications follow.

First, do not be intimidated by what the world calls power. The psalm is candid: the king is not saved by his great army. The war horse is a false hope. The political powers that loom over your news feed, the cultural forces that seem unstoppable, the corporate behemoths that shape your daily life, none of them is ultimate. God brings the counsel of the nations to nothing. He does it on his own timeline, often invisibly, but he does it. Live as someone who knows this. Do not give your fear to anything that God can dismantle with a thought.

Second, take the comfort of verse 18 into your day. “The eye of the LORD is on those who fear him.” If you fear God, if you love him, trust him, follow him, then his eye is on you in particular. Not as a generalized providence that covers everyone equally, but as the focused attention of a Father who has chosen you as his heritage. You are seen. You are watched over. You are not lost in the crowd of humanity. Whatever you are facing today, the eye of the LORD is on you.

And take the posture of verses 20-22. Wait. Trust. Hope. Receive God’s steadfast love. The Christian life is not a sprint to fix everything that is wrong. It is a long walk of waiting on the LORD who is your help and your shield. Be glad in him today. Trust his holy name. Let his steadfast love be upon you, even as you hope in him.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what feels out of control in your life or the world right now.
Thank him that nothing escapes his sight and nothing thwarts his purposes.
Ask him for a soul that waits for him.
